doc.title: Joel Dorn interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2007

title: Jazz radio's golden age versus today
summary: Dorn started on air at 19. He describes jazz disc jockeys of the late fifties and sixties, says that radio is gone, and refuses to belittle modern players.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Well I’ve always wondered, who are those people that do those little things. But your relationship with radio — I saw a quote from you it said, “if you ask me about jazz radio I’m going to make a lot of enemies.” Do you remember that?

You know I don’t remember everything that I say because a lot of it’s not worth remembering and I’m just on a constant babble. But what happened was I went on the radio when I was 19, I was a junior in college when jazz radio was pretty much on FM and it was like a new phenomenon in the late fifties through, you know, the late sixties. FM radio, nobody listened to it. It was usually the AM station simulcast or there would be a classical station every once in a while. When the jazz stations started to catch on in the late fifties and early sixties, they went on FM, it was a hip place to go. A lot of times back then when people got out of high school and they started getting into like more

serious kinds of music, jazz was one of them. It was a golden age so it was cool to dig Miles or cool to dig Brubeck or cool to dig whatever it was cool to dig. So jazz radio caught on. And it was basically a bunch of guys that dug jazz, some of whom were radio announcers, some of whom weren’t. Mostly back then the guys knew how to, you know, all jazz disc jockeys, you know had deep voices and were cool. We all spoke slowly and, you know, like that stuff. But we all loved the music and we kind of knew it. So it was a place to be. Anyway, the guys that were jazz disc jockeys back then were actually disc jockeys. Now there are a lot of people on jazz radio who are not disc jockeys, they love the music and they love to talk about it and they love to program it, but it’s not like the old days where you did ad lib commercials where you had sponsors for ten years, where you were in the clubs every night and the clubs had giants in them all the time. It was a different time and a different place. So for me I guess it’s like guys who directed film noir movies. There are no film noir movies anymore, but there were film noir movies and when there were they were the spectacular movies of their time. So jazz radio as I knew it is dead but thank God there are still people playing jazz. Does that say it? ‘Cause I don’t mean to dismiss anything of a modern time. A bunch of us were out to dinner last night, Dick LaPalma and I and like the older guys and we were with some younger guys and they love to hear the stories. And you can tell the stories and you can tell about the golden age and you can really remember something magical that happened. But if you say nothing’s happening now or, you know, then it’s kind of like condescending. A golden age is a golden age. I mean I grew up in Philly and there were three jazz clubs in Philly. And at any given time you could see Horace, Miles, Trane, Monk, and any one of a thousand other people, you know, who were coming through town on a twice a year basis. And that was when the music was in full flower.
